faq_page.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq_page.subtitle: Everything you need to know about stablecoin freezing, blacklists, and how we track on-chain censorship.
faq_page.seo_description: Frequently asked questions about stablecoin freezing, USDC and USDT blacklists, and how stables.rip tracks on-chain censorship events.
faq_page.a1: Stablecoin issuers like Circle (USDC) and Tether (USDT) have built-in blacklist functions in their smart contracts. When an address is blacklisted, the tokens at that address become permanently non-transferable. The owner cannot send, swap, or interact with those tokens in any way.
faq_page.a2: Only the issuing company can execute a freeze. Circle manages USDC blacklisting, and Tether manages USDT blacklisting. These freezes are typically initiated in response to law enforcement requests, OFAC sanctions compliance, or internal risk assessments. There is no public appeals process.
faq_page.a3: Yes. If you hold USDC in any self-custody wallet, Circle can blacklist your address at any time. This applies to Ethereum, TRON, and all other chains where USDC is deployed. The freeze is enforced at the smart contract level — no exchange or wallet app can override it.
faq_page.a4: Yes. Tether has blacklisted hundreds of addresses across Ethereum and TRON. Once blacklisted, the USDT at that address is permanently frozen. Tether has frozen over $1 billion in total across all chains.
faq_page.q5: Is freezing the same as confiscation?
faq_page.a5: Freezing prevents the address owner from moving the tokens, but the tokens are not destroyed or transferred to anyone else. They remain at the frozen address indefinitely. In some cases, law enforcement may later work with the issuer to move the frozen funds, but this is rare.
faq_page.q6: How does stables.rip track freeze events?
faq_page.a6: We monitor on-chain events from the USDC and USDT smart contracts on Ethereum and TRON. When a blacklist event (AddedBlackList, Blacklisted) is emitted, we record the address, transaction hash, timestamp, and current balance. Data is synced every 30 minutes.
faq_page.q7: Where does the data come from?
faq_page.a7: Ethereum freeze events are fetched from Etherscan's log API, monitoring the official USDT and USDC contract addresses. TRON freeze events come from the TronGrid API, monitoring the AddedBlackList events on the TRON USDT contract. Balances are verified via on-chain multicall queries.
faq_page.a8: They refer to the same thing. "Blacklisted" is the technical term used in the smart contract code. "Frozen" describes the practical effect — the tokens cannot be moved. Some blacklisted addresses show $0 balance because the tokens were moved before the freeze took effect, or were drained through other mechanisms.
faq_page.a9: Technically yes — the contracts have a removeBlackList / unBlacklist function. In practice, unfreezes are extremely rare. We track both freeze and unfreeze events when they occur.
faq_page.q10: How can I protect myself from stablecoin freezing?
faq_page.a10: The only way to fully avoid freeze risk is to not hold freezable stablecoins. Privacy-preserving cryptocurrencies like Monero (XMR) have no blacklist function, no central issuer, and no freeze capability. You can swap stablecoins for XMR without KYC at kyc.rip.
faq_page.q11: Does this affect stablecoins on exchanges?
faq_page.a11: When you hold stablecoins on a centralized exchange, the exchange holds the actual tokens in their wallet. If the exchange's wallet is frozen (rare but possible), your funds are affected. More commonly, exchanges comply with legal orders independently by freezing your account.
faq_page.a12: Currently we monitor Ethereum (ETH) and TRON for both USDT and USDC freeze events. Ethereum is where the majority of USDC freezes occur, while TRON has the most USDT blacklistings. We plan to add Arbitrum, Optimism, and Polygon monitoring in the future.
faq_page.q13: Is stables.rip affiliated with Circle or Tether?
faq_page.a13: No. stables.rip is an independent transparency project by the rip.family ecosystem (kyc.rip). We have no affiliation with any stablecoin issuer. All data is sourced from public blockchain records.
faq_page.q14: How often is the data updated?
faq_page.a14: Freeze events are synced every 30 minutes via automated cron jobs. Balance checks are performed at sync time. The "Last scan" indicator on the homepage shows when the most recent sync completed.

blacklist_page.title: Understanding Stablecoin Blacklists
blacklist_page.subtitle: How USDC and USDT freeze functions work, and what it means for your funds.
blacklist_page.seo_description: How USDC and USDT freeze functions work technically. Learn about Circle and Tether's blacklist smart contract mechanisms.
blacklist_page.usdc_p1: Circle, the issuer of USDC, maintains a blacklist function in the USDC smart contract on Ethereum (and all other chains). The blacklist(address) function can be called by Circle's designated blacklister address.
blacklist_page.usdc_p2: Once an address is blacklisted, all USDC transfers to and from that address will revert. The tokens remain at the address but are completely non-transferable. Circle has used this power to comply with OFAC sanctions, law enforcement requests, and their own risk policies.
blacklist_page.usdc_p3: Circle publishes a compliance transparency page, but the actual freeze decisions are made internally. There is no public appeal process for blacklisted addresses.
blacklist_page.usdt_p1: Tether's USDT contract on Ethereum includes addBlackList(address) and destroyBlackFunds(address) functions. Unlike USDC, Tether can not only freeze but also destroy the tokens at a blacklisted address.
blacklist_page.usdt_p2: On TRON, USDT uses the same AddedBlackList mechanism. TRON accounts for a significant portion of USDT blacklistings due to its high usage in peer-to-peer transfers.
blacklist_page.usdt_p3: Tether has historically been more aggressive with freezes than Circle. They have cooperated with law enforcement agencies globally and have frozen addresses based on DOJ requests, Interpol notices, and OFAC designations.
blacklist_page.technical_p1: Stablecoin contracts implement a modifier (often called notBlacklisted) on the transfer() and transferFrom() functions. This modifier checks a mapping of blacklisted addresses before allowing any transfer.
blacklist_page.technical_p2: When you call transfer() on USDC or USDT, the contract checks if either the sender or receiver is blacklisted. If either is, the transaction reverts. This means:
blacklist_page.technical_li1: You cannot send frozen tokens to any address
blacklist_page.technical_li2: No one can send tokens to a frozen address
blacklist_page.technical_li3: DeFi protocols cannot interact with frozen tokens
blacklist_page.technical_li4: The tokens cannot be approved for third-party spending
blacklist_page.technical_p3: The freeze is enforced at the protocol level. No wallet, DEX, or bridge can circumvent it. The only way to unfreeze is for the issuer to call the unblacklist function.
blacklist_page.why_p1: Stablecoins represent over $150 billion in market cap. They are the backbone of DeFi, cross-border payments, and crypto trading. Yet they carry a fundamental centralization risk that is often overlooked.
blacklist_page.why_p2: The freeze function means that your stablecoins are only yours as long as the issuer permits it. This is not a theoretical risk — thousands of addresses have been frozen, with billions of dollars locked.
blacklist_page.why_p3: stables.rip exists to make this reality visible. Every freeze is a data point in the ongoing story of financial censorship. Transparency is the first step toward accountability.
